Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.
slides: Welcome to a new topic, defining a new operation. It's a type of question you probably never met at school. It's new on the psychometric. But everything you need to solve it, you already know: putting a number in place of a letter, opening brackets, powers, fractions, and isolating an unknown.

slides.say: So what is a new operation? You've actually met new operations before, nobody just called them that. Imagine a little kid who sees three, then a dot, then seven. What is it? The kid has no idea. Not because they can't multiply, but because nobody told them what the dot means.
at: three, then a dot, then seven

slides: Once someone explains that the dot means times, it's easy. Three times seven is twenty-one. It was the same with the plus sign. Until someone told you that plus means adding, it was just a mark. Those were new symbols for things you already knew how to do.

slides.say: And this one really was a new operation: a small two up high, like five with a small two. Someone told you to multiply the number by itself, so five times five, twenty-five. Then you learned that a small three means three times, so two with a small three is two times two times two, which is eight. Square roots were the same story. A symbol, a definition, and then you could solve.
Now I'll teach you a brand-new operation, the heart. What is seven heart three? Right now, nobody can say, because I haven't told you what the heart does.
So let's define it. a heart b means: add a and b, and then multiply the sum by five. a is whatever sits before the heart, and b is whatever sits after it.
Seven sits before the heart, so it goes in the place of a. Three sits after it, so it goes in the place of b. Seven plus three is ten, and ten times five is fifty. So seven heart three is fifty.
at: so it goes in the place of a

slides.say: One more. Two heart six. Two goes in the place of a, and six goes in the place of b. Two plus six is eight, and eight times five is forty.

Careful to follow the whole rule. If you do seven times five, and then add three, you get thirty-eight. That's a different rule, not the heart. In the heart, the five multiplies the whole sum. That's all a new operation is: a definition, and then you follow it exactly.

On the exam, they rarely use hearts. Most of the time the symbol is a dollar sign. Sometimes it's a hash, or a special bracket. In the questions in this course you'll see a diamond. The idea is exactly the same: read the definition first, and then substitute.
at: Most of the time the symbol

slides.say: For example, diamond of a is equal to a squared minus three a. What is diamond of five? Whatever goes into the diamond takes the place of a, in every spot where a appears. Here a appears in two spots, in a squared and in three a. So we write the same template again, and put five in both spots.
at: diamond of a is equal to

slides.say: Five squared is twenty-five, and three times five is fifteen. Twenty-five minus fifteen is ten. So diamond of five is ten.
Another one, diamond of two. Again, two goes in both spots. Two squared is four, and three times two is six. Four minus six is negative two.

On the exam, they often put a negative number, or a whole expression, into the operation. So remember this rule. Whatever goes in, goes in brackets, every time. Let's take diamond of x equals x squared plus three x. What is diamond of negative two? Negative two goes in brackets, in both spots.
at: diamond of x equals x squared plus
goes in brackets, in both spots

slides.say: The bracket negative two, squared, is positive four, because a negative times a negative is positive. Three times negative two is negative six. Four minus six is negative two.
Here's the trap. Without brackets, negative two squared means the negative of two squared, which is negative four. That gives a completely different answer. With brackets, it's positive four.
Now a whole expression, x plus two. The whole x plus two goes where x was, in brackets. So diamond of x plus two is the bracket x plus two, squared, plus three times the bracket x plus two.
at: The whole x plus two goes

slides.say: Now open the brackets. The bracket x plus two, squared, is x squared plus four x plus four. Three times the bracket x plus two is three x plus six, because the three multiplies both parts. Together, that's x squared plus seven x plus ten.
Where does a new operation fit in a longer exercise? The new operation comes first, before multiplying, dividing and powers. Only brackets come before it.

Let's say diamond of x is x squared. What is diamond of three plus diamond of four? First turn each diamond into a plain number. Diamond of three is nine, and diamond of four is sixteen. Then add them. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five.

Careful, we can't join them into diamond of seven. Diamond of seven is forty-nine, a different number. Think of squares: three squared plus four squared is not seven squared. If you're not sure what comes first, ask yourself what you would do if it were a square.
But when the plus sits inside the diamond's own brackets, like diamond of, in brackets, three plus four, the brackets come first. Three plus four is seven, and diamond of seven is forty-nine.

When an operation sits inside another operation, we start with the inner brackets and work outwards, just like brackets inside brackets. Let's say diamond of x is x squared again. What is diamond of diamond of two?
at: What is diamond of diamond of two

slides.say: The inner one is diamond of two. Two squared is four. Now four takes the place of the whole inner diamond, so the outer diamond works on four. Four squared is sixteen.
at: the outer diamond works on four

slides.say: The same with an operation of two numbers. Let's define a new one, the star. a star b is three times the first number, plus the square of the second.
at: a star b is three times

slides.say: What is the bracket one star two, star three? Inner brackets first. One star two is three times one, plus two squared, so three plus four, seven. Now seven takes its place. Seven star three is three times seven, plus three squared, so twenty-one plus nine, thirty. The result of the inside becomes the input of the outside.
Another type: they don't give you the definition at all. They only say that diamond of five is thirty. Someone took five, used the diamond, and got thirty. That's all you know.

The operation could be many different things. Six x is one example, because six times five is thirty. Five x plus five is another, because twenty-five plus five is thirty. So a question like this asks which definition cannot be the operation.

Your move is to go through the choices and put five into each one. A choice that gives thirty could be the rule. The one that doesn't give thirty cannot be the rule. For example, x squared plus five gives twenty-five plus five, thirty, so it could be the rule. But four x plus eight gives twenty plus eight, twenty-eight, so it cannot.

slides: In the exam, the moment you find the one that doesn't fit, you mark it and move on. In some question videos we'll check the other choices too, just to learn.

slides.say: Back to the star: three times the first number, plus the square of the second. Two star four is six plus sixteen, twenty-two. Four star two is twelve plus four, sixteen. Swap the inputs, and you get a different answer. So don't assume a new operation behaves like plus, where the order doesn't matter. Before you calculate, check which number goes into which slot.
A question may ask: is a star b always equal to b star a? To show that it's not always true, one example where it fails is enough, like two and four.
at: To show that it's not always true

slides.say: To show that it's always true, numbers are not enough, because they only check some cases. Write the rule with letters instead. For example, b heart a is five times the bracket b plus a. And b plus a is the same as a plus b, so b heart a is always equal to a heart b. For the heart, the order never matters.
One warning for order questions: don't test with two equal numbers. Four star four equals four star four for every operation, so it can't show anything about the order.
at: don't test with two equal numbers

slides.say: And if an input is unknown? Write the definition, and it becomes an ordinary equation. For example, x star four is twenty-five. By the definition, x star four is three x plus four squared, which is three x plus sixteen. So three x plus sixteen equals twenty-five. Subtract sixteen from both sides: three x is nine, so x is three.

Let's check it. Three times three is nine, and nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. It works. One more: k heart two is thirty-five. By the definition, that's five times the bracket k plus two. So k plus two is seven, and k is five.

slides: On the exam you can also work back from the answers: put each choice into the rule, and see which one gives the result.

slides.say: Let's sum up. Read the definition, and put each input in its slot, in brackets.

Turn each operation into a number first. Nested operations go from the inside out. With no definition, test the input in each choice. For order questions, one example can show it's not always true, and letters show it's always true. Nothing complicated here, just follow the rule exactly. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
at: Turn each operation into a number first
